newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: QLD PREMIER TAKES CREDIT FOR CHANGES TO PM'S 10-POINT-PLAN
Queensland's Premier, Rob Borbidge, says the Queensland Government has forced the Prime Minister to change his 10-point-plan on native title to make it more workable.
Mr Borbidge says the plan now gives the states more flexibility to deal with the Wik issue than it did in its original form.
He's conceded the Federal government has made some concessions, but says it remains to be seen how the plan will look in legislation.
A Federal Government spokesman has welcomed Mr Borbidge's approach saying the plan is designed to give certainty to pastoralists while respecting native title.
COSTELLO SAYS GST ONLY PART OF TAX REFORM
Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says tax reform is the main issue on the agenda, and a Goods and Services Tax could be just one facet of that.
Mr Costello says his focus is to get tax rates down and ensure the burden of taxation is more evenly shared.
He told Adelaide Radio 5DN that a GST alone won't neccessarily improve the tax system.
Mr Costello says no tax is inherently better than any other, and the most important thing about a GST is its effect on other revenue raisers which are amended.
GST NOT ALL IT'S CRACKED UP TO BE
An economics academic says the concept of a goods and services tax has been greatly oversold.
The head of economics at James Cook University, Professor John Quiggan, says he can see a consumption tax being introduced if the Coalition wins a second term.
Professor Quiggan says a GST should only be considered as part of an overall tax reform package.
He says it would be an improvement, but it wouldn't solve Australia's national problems, eliminate tax evasion or greatly benefit exporters.
CREAN SAYS HOPE IS NOT LOST FOR BHP WORKERS
The Shadow Minister for Industry, Simon Crean says he hasn't given up hope that BHP's decision to shutdown steelmaking in Newcastle can be reversed.
During a visit to the city today, Mr Crean met the Lord Mayor, local industry groups and business leaders to discuss what role the Oppostion can play in the wake of BHP's decision.
Mr Crean says he'll be keeping up the pressure on the federal government to negotiate with BHP to try to keep steelmaking in the city.
STOLEN GENERATION SHOULD BE COMPENSATED
ATSIC's head says Aboriginal people taken from their families when they were children should be fairly compensated.
Gatjil Djerrkura says the so-called Stolen Generation is entitled to compensation, in the same way any other Australians who'd been through such devastation would be.
Mr Djerrkura was responding to newspaper reports suggesting the government will reject a recommedation that compensation should be paid to members of the Stolen Generation.
He says the payment of compensation would be a fair gesture.
CALL FOR GOVT TO RELEASE STOLEN GEN REPORT
Labor's Aboriginal Affairs spokesman, Daryl Melham, says there appears to be double standards in Australia in relation to the mistreatment of children.
The claim came as he accused the Federal Government of trying to smother a report on the Stolen Generation Inquiry.
The inquiry looked into the Government-backed policy of removing Aboriginal children from their families, which ended in the 1960s.
Reports today indicate the Government won't compensate the stolen children, despite the report's recommendations, and will also refuse to establish a national day of commemoration.
Mr Melham wants the report's findings tabled immediately.
He says there would be outrage if white children had been taken, and the Government was found to be sitting on a report.
Mr Melham says there has been a hue and cry about mistreatment of children by Christian Brothers recently, but Aboriginal children have been forgotten.
SCIENTIST SAYS TESTS DIDN'T CONFIRM OUTBREAK
A New Zealand scientist says tests conducted on a second outbreak of the devastating Fire Blight disease in Australia, are inconclusive
Richard Ivess has told ABC Radio, he discovered a suspicious plant in the Adelaide Botanic Gardens, and contacted the Australian Quarantine and Inspection Service.
Already the disease has been discovered in Melbourne's Botanic Gardens.
There have been reports that tests in New Zealand had confirmed the Adelaide outbreak, but Richard Ivess says that's not the case.
He says the tests were unable to isolate bacterial populations to do confirmation work.
South Australia's Primary Industries minister, Rob Kerin, says the New Zealand official's test results were always open to wide interpretation.
-- Reuter Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
